tch-b1-lesson-plan-from-objectives.q: Why does the prompt require Claude to say what to cut if the sections don't fit the class length, instead of quietly keeping everything and compressing timings?
options: It's required to generate the formative check section
Cutting is faster than compressing every section slightly
It keeps the plan realistic to the actual class length instead of aspirational and unusable in the room
It only applies to classes under 30 minutes
tch-b1-lesson-plan-from-objectives.why: Forcing an explicit time budget, with a cut list rather than silent compression, keeps the plan realistic instead of aspirational and unusable in the actual class period.

tch-b1-lesson-plan-from-objectives.q: A teacher skips giving Claude the actual class length and available materials. What's the likely result?
options: Claude will refuse to generate a plan without this information
The plan will default to a 30-minute period automatically
It has no real effect since Claude asks follow-up questions
The plan may assume resources like a computer lab or printer access the teacher doesn't actually have
tch-b1-lesson-plan-from-objectives.why: Skipping real context like class length and materials causes the plan to assume resources the teacher doesn't have, producing a generic plan that doesn't fit the actual class.

tch-b1-lesson-plan-from-objectives.q: Why does the lesson emphasize the formative check as its own required section rather than an optional add-on?
options: It's the section most likely to get skipped under time pressure, yet it's the only part that tells the teacher whether the lesson actually worked
It's required by most state curriculum standards
It automatically generates the homework assignment
It shortens the guided practice section
tch-b1-lesson-plan-from-objectives.why: The formative check is the section teachers most often skip when short on time, but it's the only part of the plan that actually reveals whether the lesson worked.

tch-b2-differentiated-materials.q: Why must the objective stay identical across the support, on-level, and extension tiers?
options: It's required for the answer key to auto-generate
Without a fixed shared objective, a 'simplified' version can quietly end up testing something easier rather than the same thing more accessibly
It's the only way Claude can format three separate PDFs
Objectives must match state testing formats exactly
tch-b2-differentiated-materials.why: Anchoring all three tiers to one stated objective is the core guardrail — otherwise a 'simplified' tier risks testing a different, easier skill instead of the same skill made more accessible.

tch-b2-differentiated-materials.q: A teacher's support-tier version strips a passage down to short factual questions requiring little analysis. What guardrail from the lesson does this violate?
options: Support tiers must always be shorter than the on-level version
Support materials should never include vocabulary scaffolds
The support tier should keep the objective's cognitive demand intact — only the language barrier should be reduced, not the thinking required
Every tier must use identical sentence structure
tch-b2-differentiated-materials.why: The lesson warns against over-simplifying the support tier until it no longer requires real thinking; rigor should stay constant while only the language load drops.

tch-b2-differentiated-materials.q: Why does the prompt require all three tiers to map onto one shared answer-key logic?
options: It's required for LMS upload compatibility
It's the only way to estimate reading level
Shared answer keys are mandated by most school districts
So the teacher can grade three physically different worksheets against the same rubric without extra work
tch-b2-differentiated-materials.why: One shared answer-key logic across tiers means the teacher can grade three different-looking worksheets consistently without building three separate rubrics.

tch-b3-quiz-assessment-generation.q: Why does the prompt require a one-line justification citing the source for every quiz answer?
options: It turns the answer key into something the teacher can audit quickly by scanning justifications against the source, instead of trusting it blindly
It's required for the quiz to print correctly
It shortens the multiple-choice options
It replaces the need for point values
tch-b3-quiz-assessment-generation.why: A citation-style justification per answer lets the teacher scan and verify the key quickly, rather than re-deriving each answer from scratch or trusting it blindly.

tch-b3-quiz-assessment-generation.q: A teacher generates a quiz and uploads it to the LMS without checking each answer against the source material. What does the lesson identify as the risk?
options: The quiz will fail to upload without verification
An AI-generated key with even one wrong answer can slip past a quick glance and cause real classroom problems
Gemini automatically re-checks all answers before allowing upload
This is only a risk for short-answer questions, not multiple choice
tch-b3-quiz-assessment-generation.why: The lesson calls out skipping line-by-line verification of the key as the single most important step to not skip, since even one wrong answer can cause real classroom problems.

tch-b3-quiz-assessment-generation.q: Why does the prompt ask for wrong multiple-choice options based on plausible, common misconceptions rather than random distractors?
options: Random distractors are against most testing standards
It's required to balance point values across questions
It produces better multiple-choice options than a teacher might write under time pressure, without inventing anything outside the source
Plausible distractors are easier for Gemini to generate quickly
tch-b3-quiz-assessment-generation.why: Distractors grounded in common misconceptions make the multiple-choice questions more diagnostic than arbitrary wrong answers, without inventing facts outside the source.

tch-i1-feedback-comments.q: Why does the prompt require pasting actual quotes from the student's work rather than just a rubric score?
options: Quotes are required to calculate the final grade
It shortens the feedback to under 100 words
It's needed to detect plagiarism in the student's work
Without real quotes, the model has nothing to reference but adjectives, producing a generic compliment instead of specific feedback
tch-i1-feedback-comments.why: Grounding the comment in real quotes is what separates specific, useful feedback from a generic compliment, since the model otherwise has nothing concrete to reference.

tch-i1-feedback-comments.q: Why does the prompt explicitly ban inventing examples from the student's work that weren't provided?
options: The model never saw the actual paper and will otherwise produce a plausible-sounding but fabricated detail
Invented examples take longer to generate
It's required to keep comments under the word limit
Fabricated examples are considered too harsh in tone
tch-i1-feedback-comments.why: Since the model never actually saw the student's paper, it will produce a plausible but fabricated example unless explicitly told to use only the quotes and notes provided.

tch-i1-feedback-comments.q: Why does the glow/grow/next-step structure pair one strength and one weakness with a single concrete next step, rather than an exhaustive list of issues?
options: It's required to fit the 120-180 word limit only
A single actionable next step is more useful to a student than an overwhelming list, pairing recognition with one clear change
Exhaustive lists are against most schools' grading policies
It reduces the time needed to read the rubric
tch-i1-feedback-comments.why: The glow/grow/next-step pattern pairs recognition with one actionable change, which is more useful to a student than an overwhelming list of every issue at once.

tch-i2-parent-communication-templates.q: Why does the prompt keep templates deliberately generic with bracketed placeholders instead of any invented specific details?
options: Generic templates are required by most school communication policies
Placeholders are the only way to personalize for phone use
A template with fabricated detail risks being sent as-is by mistake, potentially referencing a student or incident that isn't real
It shortens the template below 120 words automatically
tch-i2-parent-communication-templates.why: Keeping templates generic with placeholders avoids the risk of a template containing invented specifics being sent as-is by mistake.

tch-i2-parent-communication-templates.q: Why must every concern-type message end with a collaborative next step rather than just stating the issue?
options: It's a legal requirement for parent communication
It's needed to keep the tone warm regardless of content
Next steps are only required for repeat-issue messages
Without a next step, the message reads as a pure complaint instead of something constructive to move forward on together
tch-i2-parent-communication-templates.why: Requiring a collaborative next step keeps concern messages constructive rather than reading as a complaint with nothing actionable to do next.

tch-i2-parent-communication-templates.q: Why does the lesson recommend a separate, sharper template version for repeat issues versus first-time issues?
options: A repeat pattern calls for a different level of directness than a first-time issue, and composing that harder message cold, under stress, is worse than having it ready
Repeat-issue templates are required to be shorter
First-time templates don't need placeholders
It's only relevant for grade-concern messages
tch-i2-parent-communication-templates.why: A repeat pattern genuinely calls for more directness than a first-time issue, and having that sharper version ready ahead of time beats composing it cold under stress.

tch-i3-notebooklm-curriculum-knowledge-b.q: Why is a Claude Project particularly well suited to a standards-coverage gap analysis, compared to a general chat outside a project?
options: It can generate lesson plans faster than other tools
It grounds every answer in the specific documents uploaded to the project, so claims can be traced and verified against your own material rather than Claude's general training data
It automatically writes new unit plans without teacher review
It has no character limit on uploaded documents
tch-i3-notebooklm-curriculum-knowledge-b.why: A Claude Project's uploaded knowledge lets every claim be traced to the exact document you provided, which matters enormously for a consequential task like certifying standards coverage.

tch-i3-notebooklm-curriculum-knowledge-b.q: A teacher gets an answer from Claude listing uncovered standards but never checks it against the source document. What problem does this create?
options: The answer will be automatically flagged as unverified by Claude
It has no real downside since Claude never makes mistakes
It defeats the entire point of grounding the project in your own documents, which exists specifically so the teacher can verify each claim
Grounding only works for uploaded PDFs, not other file types
tch-i3-notebooklm-curriculum-knowledge-b.why: Not checking the answer against the source document defeats the entire point of grounding the project in your own uploaded material, which exists specifically so claims can be verified, not just trusted.

tch-i3-notebooklm-curriculum-knowledge-b.q: Why does the lesson recommend a separate Claude Project per course rather than one giant project for everything a teacher teaches?
options: Claude limits the number of documents per project to a handful
Separate projects are required for FERPA compliance
It reduces the number of citations generated per answer
Grounded answers get noticeably sharper against a focused, relevant source set
tch-i3-notebooklm-curriculum-knowledge-b.why: A focused, course-specific source set produces noticeably sharper grounded answers than one giant project mixing material from everything a teacher teaches.

tch-a1-ai-resilient-assignments-literacy.q: Why does the lesson recommend redesigning assignments around specific in-class or personal evidence rather than relying on AI-detection software?
options: AI-detection software is unreliable, has a real false-positive rate, and teaches students nothing, while requiring evidence generic AI can't produce actually resists ghostwriting
Detection software is banned in most school districts
Detection software only works for essays, not other assignment types
In-class evidence is faster for teachers to grade
tch-a1-ai-resilient-assignments-literacy.why: The lesson explicitly warns against relying on AI-detection software as a main defense, since it's unreliable and has real false positives, unlike redesigning around evidence generic AI can't produce.

tch-a1-ai-resilient-assignments-literacy.q: Why does the redesigned assignment include 2-3 checkpoint deliverables spaced across the timeline?
options: Checkpoints are required for the assignment to count as a major grade
The redesign only works if the student's process is visible over time, not just the final product
It reduces the total length of the final submission
It's the only way to add a formative check to the assignment
tch-a1-ai-resilient-assignments-literacy.why: Staged checkpoints make the student's own process visible over time, which is the actual mechanism that resists AI ghostwriting, not just checking the final product.

tch-a1-ai-resilient-assignments-literacy.q: A teacher writes an AI-use policy stating only 'don't use AI dishonestly' with no concrete examples. What problem does the lesson identify with this approach?
options: Vague policies are against school district legal requirements
This is actually the recommended approach for older students
A policy too vague for students to genuinely tell what's allowed produces more violations, not fewer
It has no real effect since students read the fine print elsewhere
tch-a1-ai-resilient-assignments-literacy.why: The lesson warns that a policy vague enough that students can't tell what's actually allowed produces more violations, not fewer, since the line is never made concrete.

stu-b1-ai-tutor-without-cheating.q: Why does the prompt require the student to write out their own understanding of the topic before asking Claude anything?
options: It's required for Claude to detect the subject area
It shortens the overall tutoring session
It's needed to select the correct difficulty level
Retrieving what you already know before getting new instruction improves retention far more than instruction alone
stu-b1-ai-tutor-without-cheating.why: Writing your own explanation first is the highest-leverage part of the prompt, since retrieval before new instruction improves retention far more than instruction alone.

stu-b1-ai-tutor-without-cheating.q: A student gets stuck and immediately asks for the full answer instead of a small hint. What does the lesson say about this?
options: Asking for the full answer the moment it gets hard is a common mistake that defeats the purpose of Socratic tutoring
This is the correct approach once a student has tried for more than a minute
Full answers are fine as long as the student re-reads them afterward
It only matters for exam-related studying, not homework
stu-b1-ai-tutor-without-cheating.why: The lesson lists asking for the full answer the moment it gets hard, instead of requesting a small hint, as a common mistake that undermines the tutoring method.

stu-b1-ai-tutor-without-cheating.q: Why does the prompt ask the student to explain the topic back, from memory, after receiving the full explanation?
options: It's required to generate a grade for the session
It closes the loop and reveals whether real understanding actually landed, rather than just recognition of a correct-looking explanation
It's the only way to save the conversation for later
It replaces the need for class notes
stu-b1-ai-tutor-without-cheating.why: Explaining the topic back from memory closes the learning loop and reveals whether genuine understanding landed, rather than just passive recognition of a correct explanation.

stu-b2-summarize-question-readings.q: Why is uploading the actual reading to Claude preferred over asking for a summary from general knowledge?
options: Without an uploaded file, Claude cannot produce any summary at all
It requires a paid subscription for summaries
A general answer risks drifting from what the text actually says by filling gaps from general training data, while uploading the reading grounds every claim in the actual document
Uploading is faster at generating summaries
stu-b2-summarize-question-readings.why: Without the uploaded reading, an answer risks drifting from the actual text by filling gaps from general training data; uploading the document grounds every claim in the specific text.

stu-b2-summarize-question-readings.q: A student uploads a summary of the reading they found online instead of the actual assigned text. What problem does this create?
options: Claude will automatically reject non-original uploads
It has no real effect as long as the summary is accurate
It only matters for citation-heavy readings like research papers
It defeats the grounding entirely, since Claude can only work from what's actually uploaded, not the real source
stu-b2-summarize-question-readings.why: Uploading someone else's summary instead of the actual assigned reading defeats the grounding entirely, since Claude can only draw from what was actually uploaded.

stu-b2-summarize-question-readings.q: Why does the prompt ask for both factual recall questions and 'explain why/how' questions rather than just recall questions?
options: It mirrors how most exams actually test material at two different depths, so the self-quiz doesn't just check surface recall
Explain-why questions are required for Claude to cite the source text
It shortens the number of questions needed overall
Recall-only questions are against most academic integrity policies
stu-b2-summarize-question-readings.why: Mixing recall and explain-why/how questions mirrors how exams actually test material at two depths, so the self-quiz checks real understanding, not just surface recall.

stu-b3-exam-prep-practice-spaced-review.q: Why does the schedule revisit earlier topics at increasing intervals rather than reviewing everything equally every day?
options: Increasing intervals are required to fit within a fixed number of days
Revisiting material just as you start to forget it, after a genuine retrieval attempt, produces much stronger long-term retention than passive re-reading
It reduces the total number of practice questions needed
It's only effective for math and science subjects
stu-b3-exam-prep-practice-spaced-review.why: Spaced repetition works because revisiting material right as you start to forget it, after real retrieval, produces much stronger retention than passive re-reading on a fixed daily schedule.

stu-b3-exam-prep-practice-spaced-review.q: A student takes the practice quiz with their notes open next to them. What problem does this create?
options: Open-book practice is fine as long as the schedule is still followed
It only matters for the final practice round before the exam
It destroys the point of active recall, which is the actual mechanism that improves retention
Nothing — open-book practice produces the same learning benefit
stu-b3-exam-prep-practice-spaced-review.why: Taking the practice test open-book destroys the point of active recall, which is the core mechanism that makes practice testing effective for retention.

stu-b3-exam-prep-practice-spaced-review.q: Why does the prompt instruct the AI to ask the student rather than assume when the exam might cover a topic not in their notes?
options: It's required to keep the practice set under 15 questions
Assumed topics are automatically flagged as incorrect by ChatGPT
Adding unconfirmed topics risks studying material that isn't actually on the exam, wasting limited study time
It's only relevant for open-note exams
stu-b3-exam-prep-practice-spaced-review.why: Letting the AI add exam topics never actually given to it risks studying material that may not be on the exam, wasting limited and valuable study time.

stu-i1-writing-feedback-not-ghostwriting.q: Why is the 'describe, don't rewrite' rule the core guardrail in this lesson, even for a single example sentence?
options: The moment the model generates replacement sentences, even as an example, that language can end up in the student's final draft, crossing into ghostwriting
Rewritten sentences take longer for Claude to generate
It's required to keep the feedback under a word limit
Descriptive feedback is easier for teachers to grade
stu-i1-writing-feedback-not-ghostwriting.why: The 'describe, don't rewrite' rule is what keeps this on the feedback side of the academic-integrity line, since any generated replacement language risks ending up in the final draft.

stu-i1-writing-feedback-not-ghostwriting.q: A student asks Claude to rewrite a paragraph 'just to see' and then keeps some of that language in their final submission. What does the lesson identify about this?
options: This is acceptable as long as the student cites Claude as a source
This is the actual boundary that gets students in academic-integrity trouble, even though it started as a curiosity check
It's only a problem if the whole paragraph is used, not a few words
Institutions generally allow this under fair-use policies
stu-i1-writing-feedback-not-ghostwriting.why: The lesson names this exact pattern — asking for a rewrite 'just to see' and keeping some of that language — as the actual boundary that causes real academic-integrity trouble.

stu-i1-writing-feedback-not-ghostwriting.q: Why does the lesson recommend checking your institution's AI policy before starting, rather than assuming feedback-only use is always fine?
options: Institutions require a separate account for AI feedback tools
Policy checks are needed to unlock Claude's feedback mode
AI policies vary widely between institutions and courses, and this lesson assumes feedback and editing help is permitted, not something to take for granted
It's only relevant for graduate-level writing
stu-i1-writing-feedback-not-ghostwriting.why: The lesson explicitly notes that AI policies vary widely and that its guidance assumes feedback and editing help is permitted, so checking first is necessary, not optional.

stu-i2-research-papers-find-organize-syn.q: Why is verifying every AI-suggested source before citing it described as non-optional in this lesson?
options: Verification is only required for sources older than 2015
It's needed to format citations in the correct style
Unverified sources are automatically removed by Gemini before output
Language models can generate plausible-looking but fabricated citations, making personal verification the core safeguard against a fake reference in the bibliography
stu-i2-research-papers-find-organize-syn.why: Language models can generate plausible-looking but fabricated citations, so personally verifying every suggested source is the core safeguard against a fake reference ending up in the paper.

stu-i2-research-papers-find-organize-syn.q: A student copies the AI's one-sentence description of a source directly into their paper as their synthesis. What's wrong with this?
options: That's the AI's summary of the title/abstract, not the student's own synthesis after actually reading and engaging with the source
It's fine as long as the source is cited correctly
One-sentence descriptions are considered plagiarism-proof
This is the intended use of the description field
stu-i2-research-papers-find-organize-syn.why: The one-sentence description is only meant to help the student know what to look for when reading; it's not a substitute for the student's own synthesis after actually reading the source.

stu-i2-research-papers-find-organize-syn.q: Why does the lesson recommend asking specifically for a source that disagrees with the student's working thesis?
options: Disagreeing sources are required to meet most citation-count minimums
Papers built only on supporting sources usually have a weaker argument than ones that also engage a real counterpoint
It's needed to avoid citing the same author twice
It shortens the overall research process
stu-i2-research-papers-find-organize-syn.why: Papers built only on supporting sources tend to have weaker arguments than ones that also engage a genuine counterpoint, which is why seeking disagreement is recommended.

stu-i3-learn-technical-skill-practice-lo.q: Why does the prompt insist on one problem at a time, with no solution shown until two failed attempts?
options: It's required to keep the conversation within Claude's context limit
One problem at a time is faster for Claude to generate
It forces the retrieval effort that builds durable skill — without it, a student would pattern-match off a shown solution instead of solving it themselves
It's only necessary for coding-related skills
stu-i3-learn-technical-skill-practice-lo.why: The one-problem, no-early-solution constraint forces the genuine retrieval effort that builds durable skill, rather than letting the student pattern-match off a shown answer.

stu-i3-learn-technical-skill-practice-lo.q: Why does the feedback reference the student's specific attempt rather than giving a generic explanation of the concept?
options: Generic explanations are against the tool's formatting rules
It's required to advance to a harder problem
It shortens the time spent on each problem
Referencing the actual attempt makes each round of feedback useful instead of repetitive, and pinpoints exactly what the student got wrong
stu-i3-learn-technical-skill-practice-lo.why: Feedback tied to the student's actual attempt is specific and useful, pinpointing the real error, unlike a generic explanation that would feel repetitive across rounds.

stu-i3-learn-technical-skill-practice-lo.q: A student picks 'learn calculus' as their practice topic instead of something like 'find the derivative of a polynomial.' What problem does this create?
options: A topic that broad is too unfocused to generate a well-calibrated, right-sized practice problem
It only matters if the student is a beginner
Claude will automatically narrow the topic on its own
Broad topics are fine as long as the student specifies a grade level
stu-i3-learn-technical-skill-practice-lo.why: The lesson lists picking a skill too broad, like 'learn calculus,' as a common mistake, since it's too unfocused to generate a well-calibrated practice problem.

stu-a1-personal-learning-system.q: Why does the prompt ask the AI to flag if the student's course load doesn't realistically fit their available hours, rather than fitting everything in anyway?
options: It's required to calculate a GPA estimate
A plan that assumes more time than a student actually has gets abandoned in week one
Flagging is needed to unlock the weekly checkpoint feature
It shortens the plan to a single page automatically
stu-a1-personal-learning-system.why: The honest-hours check matters because a plan that assumes more available time than a student actually has tends to get abandoned within the first week.

stu-a1-personal-learning-system.q: Why does the plan rotate spaced review across all of a student's courses each week, not just the one with the nearest deadline?
options: Rotation is required to keep each course's notebook under a size limit
It's only relevant for students taking more than 5 courses
Focusing only on the nearest deadline lets review lapse on other courses, undermining the retention benefit of spaced review across the whole term
Nearest-deadline focus is actually the recommended approach
stu-a1-personal-learning-system.why: The lesson lists only applying techniques to whichever course has the nearest deadline, instead of rotating spaced review across all courses, as a common mistake.

stu-a1-personal-learning-system.q: Why does the lesson include a weekly checkpoint question ('what did I forget that I knew last week?') as part of the system?
options: It's required to generate the following week's practice problems
Checkpoint questions are needed to sync with NotebookLM
It replaces the need for a written weekly plan
It turns the plan into something actively revised based on evidence, instead of a plan set once and quietly abandoned
stu-a1-personal-learning-system.why: The weekly checkpoint question is what turns the system into something actively revised based on real evidence, rather than a plan set once and never adjusted.
